newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US durables seen up, hint steady growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US durables seen up, hint steady growth.

text.p: The U.S. January durable goods report will likely show a rebound from recent losses, suggesting the economy's manufacturing sector continues to grow moderately, economists said.

"The story you continue to get from this series ... is that durable goods are holding up well, suggesting it's going to be supportive of a continued expansion," said William Griggs, managing director at Griggs and Santow Inc.
The durable goods orders report will be released on Thursday, February 27, at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
In a Reuters poll, analysts forecast the overall number will rise by 1.5 percent in January against a 1.9 percent drop in December.
The ex-defense data is expected to be up 2.2 percent against a 1.8 percent drop in the previous month.
Analysts said gains are expected throughout the report, but they pointed to electrical machinery and transportation as the main sectors leading the upward trend in January.
"We're looking for a pretty sharp increase in durable goods orders," said Brian Jones, director of economic and market analysis at Salomon Brothers.

"What we have driving this report up is a snap back for machinery orders and an automotive-led rebound in transportation equipment," he added. Jones expects a 4.0 percent increase in overall durable goods orders in January.

Analysts said machinery orders were abnormally weak in the last two months. "It has been weak and I think we're going to get a snap back in January," said Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.
Wall Street experts said the recent weakness in electrical machinery was not related to slowing computer sales.
"It wasn't computers. It was primarily communications equipment and I think it's because those orders tend to be very lumpy," Salomon's Jones said.
Analysts said the expected rise in durable goods orders in January is related to seasonal factors and it does not imply pent-up demand is increasing.
"I think there isn't a lot of pent-up demand in any area," Griggs and Santow's Griggs said.

"I think demand it's pretty well taken care of in housing, autos ... Things are there and people are pretty much satisfied. I don't think (pent-up demand) is a big player in this picture now," Griggs added.
Analysts said financial markets are expected to have a mute reaction to the numbers if they come in in line with expectations.

Some of them also said that Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday was likely to overshadow the importance of the durables data to the market this month.
"Depending on what the chairman says tomorrow you might end up getting a favorable or negative response to the numbers," said a money trader at a U.S. bank.
"I think that whatever Greenspan says will end up influencing the way people will look at the numbers on Thursday," he added.
